claims.statement: The MCP introduction describes a standard for connecting model applications with context sources and tools and says it can extend the cloud agent. Standardization alone does not prove compatibility, trustworthiness, authorized access or safe execution of a particular server.

The task form describes selecting a repository, entering a prompt and optional visual inputs in PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP formats, then optionally choosing a base branch for a new branch. Prompt/image examples were not submitted; a repository selector does not establish mutation authority.

The task form includes optional custom-agent selection or creation at repository/organization/enterprise scope and optional model selection, with reasoning selection conditional on model support. Its nested gate says third-party agents require paid plans; none of these options proves target entitlement or authorizes paid usage.

The form's start action is described as creating a session and pushing code changes, with pull-request creation requested in the prompt or initiated from session logs. Viewing or filling a form is distinct from actually starting, pushing or opening a pull request; no remote agent was launched.

The Raycast introduction describes a Windows/macOS launcher integration for starting and tracking cloud-agent tasks and viewing live logs. This is a pinned capability claim, not verified installation, platform behavior or a running session.

The Raycast restriction note gives organization OAuth-app restrictions as a possible reason a repository cannot be selected and directs an approval request. It is not a definitive diagnosis or authority to bypass restrictions or grant approval.

The Raycast setup fragment names launcher installation and a separate Copilot extension installation. Links are not software integrity verification; neither installation nor upstream setup execution occurred.

The hook troubleshooting table checks location under .github/hooks, valid JSON, version 1, executable script status and shebang. These are diagnostic suggestions rather than sufficient proof of hook safety, actual execution or authorization to change file permissions.
The hook timeout guidance gives a 30-second default and suggests timeoutSec changes or reducing unnecessary work. Increasing a timeout is not guaranteed repair, and no configuration was changed.
The hook output guidance calls for single-line JSON with Unix compaction or Windows compressed serialization; parseable JSON is not semantic correctness, safe output or contract completeness.

The debugging examples enable shell tracing, read standard input and print it to stderr, which can disclose sensitive prompt/tool data. Local example invocations and exit/output inspection are illustrative only; untrusted hooks were not executed and no private inputs logged.
